meta_description: New England Shirt Company has sewn dress and sport shirts in Fall River, MA since 1933, one of America's last working domestic shirt factories.
lead: One of the last operating shirt factories in America, cutting and sewing in Fall River, Massachusetts since 1933.

sections.verdict: Yes, emphatically. New England Shirt Company is not a fashion brand; it's a working factory that also sells direct, and the shirts reflect that: well-made, unpretentious, built to be worn rather than collected. If you want a dress shirt or a heavy flannel cut and sewn by American union workers in a building that has been doing exactly this since 1933, there are very few places left where that's genuinely true, and at $128–$198, the value is real.
sections.commitment: Everything is made in Fall River. The factory employs skilled sewers who work the same floor, the same machinery, and the same methods that have defined the building since the Roosevelt administration. There is no offshore component, no finishing done elsewhere. The label says "Made in USA" and it means it, down to the cut, the stitch, and the button.
sections.character: New England Shirt Company isn't just a label. It's a factory first, and that distinction matters. The building on Alden Street has been cutting shirts since 1933, and today it operates as a contract manufacturer for upwards of 150 brands and retailers. Thom Browne and Epaulet have both relied on the factory for private-label production. Most famously, when Ralph Lauren needed shirts for the 2016 U.S. Olympic team uniforms, they called Fall River: the factory produced 6,000 button-downs for the 558 American athletes. That contract work isn't just a bragging right. It keeps the workforce employed year-round and gives the factory the volume it needs to stay viable.
sections.ethics: When Bob Kidder rescued the factory in 2009, he rehired a significant portion of the union workforce, a deliberate choice, not an afterthought. Kidder has been publicly vocal about the importance of domestic manufacturing and American jobs, and the factory's continued employment of union workers is consistent with that position. The contract manufacturing model does mean that some shirts bearing this factory's construction are sold under other labels without that origin disclosed, worth knowing if full supply chain transparency matters to you. We've reached out to New England Shirt Company for more detail on wages and labor conditions and will update this section when we hear back.
sections.heritage: The factory began operations in 1933 inside the historic Flint Mills complex, a sprawling brick mill building in Fall River, MA that was built when Fall River was the cotton textile capital of the United States. It survived the long deindustrialization of New England's textile industry, came within inches of permanent closure in 2009, and is still running today. That's not a marketing narrative; it's a genuine anomaly. Most factories like this one are gone. This one isn't.
sections.value: Sport shirts and Oxfords typically run $128 to $178, with heavier flannels reaching $188 to $198. The factory runs periodic warehouse sales and occasional buy-3-get-1 promotions, which can bring the effective per-shirt cost down meaningfully if you're buying in volume. Compared to imported shirts at department store prices, that's a premium. Compared to what you'd pay for a made-in-USA shirt from a heritage brand spending heavily on marketing, it's fair, and you're paying for actual domestic factory labor, not the story wrapped around it.
